system_prompt:
You are extracting load-bearing passages from one chapter of a guitar method book.

The user will give you the verbatim text of one chapter. Extract every passage
that does any of the following:

- teaches a technique (how to play, fingering, hand position, picking pattern)
- defines a concept (a chord type, a scale, a position system, a terminology)
- gives a rule (when to do X, what to avoid, what to prefer)
- shows a load-bearing example (an exercise that illustrates a method's
  characteristic move)

Output a JSON object with this shape:

  { "quotes": [
      { "topic": "<short topic label>",
        "verbatim_quote": "<exact substring of the input>",
        "why_load_bearing": "<one sentence on why this passage matters>",
        "page": <int, optional>
      },
      ...
  ] }

CRITICAL RULES:
1. `verbatim_quote` MUST be an EXACT substring of the input text. Do not
   paraphrase. Do not add words. Do not fix typos. Copy character-for-character.
2. If you can't find a substantial passage in the input that fits a topic,
   skip the topic — don't fabricate.
3. Skip prose that is purely biographical, motivational, or transitional.
   Keep prose that teaches.
4. Aim for 3-15 quotes per chapter. A chapter with only one load-bearing
   passage gets one quote; a dense chapter gets many.
5. `topic` is a short label (2-6 words). Use the book's own terminology
   when possible.
6. `why_load_bearing` is one sentence in YOUR voice explaining the
   significance — not a paraphrase of the quote.

          mother to take him to a guitar teacher. So he began studying guitar with José Walter, which
          gave him the first basic steps to rock and blues.

How to use this book
Although a big part of this method is exclusively dedicated to the guitar, (because it refers to
chord construction and basic visualization of the guitar fretboard),it was created as a tool for all
instruments of all levels (beginner, intermediate and advanced). However, even if you are an
advanced player, make sure you know start at the beginning of the book, otherwise you will
easily get lost by the end of the book.


This method should be used as a dictionary of ideas and techniques. It's important to understand
that the way we approach the musical concepts, ideas and techniques presented here are unique
and cannot be found elsewhere.


Do not worry about learning everything from every chapter. You can go ahead as soon as you
understand the concepts. But always remember that you can come back to any chapter of any
book in order to learn more about a determined subject you want to study again.


Be careful when trying to learn too much at one time. Music is not about quantity but quality.

    Harmony Knowledge and Rules

    Harmonic Regions for Major Keys
    The Harmonic Regions de1ine and organize the roles of each chord with regard to the key
    of a song, in addition to providing various replacement options for each of them. We have
    3 harmonic regions: ("C" major as reference)


    1- Root Region Chords (Tonic): Cmaj7 (I), Em7 (IIIm), Am7 (VIm).
    2- Subdominant Region Chords: (this group in divided into two groups):
    • Major: Fmaj7 (IV), Dm7 (IIm), Bbmaj7 (bVII).
    • Minor: Fm7(6) (7+) (IVm), Bb7 (bVII), Abmaj7 (bVI), Dbmaj7 (bII).

    3- Dominant Region Chords: G7 (V), Bø (VII).
                                  68


    Functions of the Harmonic Regions:
                         46




    • Root Region(Tonic):
     It gives the sense of resolution, rest or "being home" (key).

    • Subdominant Region:
     It gives the sense of movement and distancing, moving away from the tonic.

    • Dominant Region:
    It gives the sense of tension and instability, and wants to resolve to the tonic. With these three
    functions ( IV / V / I = distancing, tension and rest ), we generate what we call a cadence, which
    is a chord progression with a resolution effect that defines the music's path. So let's understand
    some aspects of this:

    Substitution Chords using Harmonic Regions:                                                           4668




    In theory, any chord of a given Harmonic Region may be replaced by another of the same region.
    Hence we will find the most famous cadence in popular music: IIm / V/ I. But notice that we
    had to replace the IVth degree by the IIm, which belongs to the same region.
    It is important to understand that a cadence does not have to be completed all the time.
    Sometimes we cannot play II / V/ I in the same bar, therefore we can simply play V/ I. Actually,
    a subdominant chord is used to delay the Dominant chord, giving more colors to the harmony.
    In addition to the substitutions we can make between chords derived from the same Harmonic
    Region,we can also go deeper with substitutions by replacing chords derived from the Dominant
    Region with the ones derived from the Major or Minor Subdominant Region.

    Attention in the exercises below:
    a) I covers all the chords derived from the Root Region.
    b) V covers all the chords derived from the Dominant Region.
    c) IV covers all the chords derived from the Subdominant Region.

                                                                                                      4668




In minor keys we may use the Harmonic Regions as follows (“Cm” as reference):

1- Root Region Chords: Cm7 (I), Ebmaj7 (bIII)

3- Dominant Region Chords: G7 (V), B˚ (VII)


Attention:

In minor keys the chords of the Dominant Region can be replaced by the chords of the Minor
Subdominant Region. Moreover, in a more modern view, we can also use the chords belonging
to the Minor Subdominant Region of the relative major key to replace the chords from the
Dominant Region. The examples given here are in the key of Cm, so we would use the chords
of the Minor Subdominant Region of "Eb" major replacing the chords from the Dominant
Region (G7, B˚).

An important detail to notice in the cadence II/V/I in minor keys (IVm/V7/Im) is that the
dominant seventh chords almost always use altered tensions such as: b9, # 9, # 11, b13. The
major 13th can be used with some regularity in the chords, but it is still an exception. In the key
of Cm we can have the cadence: G7(b9)13 leading to Cm7 for example.

Even though there are many possibilities, we can never forget that the most important thing
when comping is to follow the melody, which will “tell” us what the best chord options are.
However, when improvising we can be more free because we will create the melodies, so it
means that even if we have a pre-set harmony dictated by the music, we can use all the “colors”
we have learned before, playing single notes or even block chords.

• Basic Major II / V / I Progression:                         Dmi7          G7        Cmaj7    ‘
• Basic Minor II / V / I Progression:                         Dª            G7        Cmi7     ‘

It is important to understand that any tension note applyed over these chords (7, 9, 11, 13), does
not affect their function in any way. Actually the tension notes are used to "color" the cadence.

Similarity between the major and the minor II/V/I cadences:
Despite being apparently two very different chord progressions, there is a huge correlation
between the major and the minor II/V/I cadences. Therefore, in order to better understand that
idea, let's analize them degree by degree for comparison.

The comparison between both cadences can only work if we use them in the right keys. Let’s
use the keys of “C” major and “Am”, because they are relatives and this is the beginning of the
similarity we are looking for. See below:

•     Dmi7       G7      Cmaj7          ‘                 •          Bª        Emi7     Ami7   ‘

II degree = Dm7 is a dorian chord, which means that it could be Dm6 as well. Now comes the
tricky thing: the third inversion of Dm6 is Bø which is the II degree from the Am cadence. So
we conclude that both II degree are the same.
                                68


V degree = Considering that G7(b9) is an option of the V chord leading to C major, and E7(b9)
is an option of the V degree leading to Am, we can compare them properly. So, first of all we
                      46




must understand that G7(b9) is the same chord as Ab˚ with a different root. See below:

• G7(b9) : G, B, D, F, Ab           • Ab˚ : Ab, B, D, F

The diminished chord repeats itself every minor 3rd. So Ab˚ = B˚= D˚ = F˚. Now let's
understand that E7(b9)/B is the same chord as B˚. So, finally we have Ab˚ = B˚ or G7(b9) =
E7(b9). Other tensions applied over these 2 dominant 7th chords can work with this comparison
as well, but the flat 9 is the best example. Later on we will better understand that correlation
between both cadences.

I degree = “Am” is the relative minor of “C major”, therefore the same chord (C6).

Conclusion: We may then conclude that both II/V/I progressions can be considered the
same depending on the treatment given to the chords.
